extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of early modern philosophy (Locke) / scholars of epistemology
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of John Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding (chapters on simple ideas and origins of knowledge), summarising his claims about how ideas arise and their classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness as essential to thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Thinking consists in being conscious that one thinks; to suppose the soul thinks while the man is not conscious of it is unintelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke objects to the idea that the soul may 'always think' while the man is not aware: consciousness (perception of what passes in one's own mind) is necessary to count as thinking. He argues we have no access to another's consciousness and that ordinary experience doesn't support thinking without awareness (examples: waking a sleeper; animals that show behaviour but cannot tell us they think).

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of all ideas: Sensation and Reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: No ideas but from Sensation and Reflection — the impressions from outward objects and the mind's own operations about those impressions are the original of all knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke's central thesis: ideas in the understanding are coeval with sensation (impressions from external objects) and reflection (the mind reflecting on its own operations). Even the most sublime thoughts are built from these materials; our intellectual faculties recombine but do not go beyond these inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical evidence from children: no innate ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation of children shows few signs of habitual thinking or reasoning at birth; this supports denying innate ideas or an always-thinking soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke urges reliance on observation and experience rather than hypothesis: newborns and fetuses show little perception or reasoning, spend most time asleep, and thus provide evidence that ideas arise after sensory experience, not innate possession of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind's thinking increases with sensory matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind thinks in proportion to the matter it gets from experience to think about; as senses furnish ideas, the mind becomes more awake and capable of remembering, imagining, and reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke suggests progressive development: as a child acquires sensory impressions and retains them, the faculties of memory, imagination, reasoning, and abstraction improve by exercise and composition of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas begin with sensation; definition of sensation
rubrics_metrics.description: A man begins to have ideas when he first has any sensation; sensation is an impression or motion made in some part of the body, noticed in the understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke locates the origin of first ideas in bodily impressions that are perceived by the understanding — sensation is the initial source that supplies the mind with material for ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reception of simple ideas: the understanding is passive
rubrics_metrics.description: In the reception of simple ideas the understanding is for the most part passive; the mind cannot refuse, alter, or obliterate simple ideas when they are imprinted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke compares the mind to a mirror: objects of the senses impress simple ideas on the mind without the mind's active construction. Many external objects 'obtrude' ideas whether we will or not, producing obscure notions even when unattended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: simple ideas vs complex ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Some ideas are SIMPLE (uncompounded appearances) and some are COMPLEX; simple ideas are uniform and not distinguishable into different ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although sensory qualities in objects are blended, the simple ideas they produce in the mind enter as distinct and unmixed (e.g., coldness and hardness vs smell and whiteness). Complex ideas are compounded later by the understanding from simple ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind cannot invent or destroy simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The understanding has no power to invent or frame one new simple idea not received from sensation or reflection, nor to destroy those it has.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues that no amount of wit or thought can create a new simple idea (e.g., a taste or scent never experienced). He uses examples (blind man imagining colours, deaf man imagining sounds) to show the limits of imagination regarding simple sensory qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only qualities affecting the senses are imaginable
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the qualities that affect the senses (sight, hearing, taste, smell, touch) are imaginable; we cannot imagine other qualities unless we had the relevant sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke allows that other creatures might have more senses, but for humans only qualities conveyed by our senses are available to imagination and conception. He cautions against presuming human senses are exhaustive of all possible faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of simple ideas by source
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple ideas can be divided by how they approach the mind: (1) by one sense only, (2) by more than one sense, (3) from reflection only, (4) by both sensation and reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke proposes to consider ideas separately according to these sources. Examples: colours (one sense), space/extension (sight and touch), operations of the mind (reflection), and some ideas present via multiple routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of solidity derived from touch (resistance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of solidity is received by our touch and arises from the resistance we find in bodies to the entrance of any other body into the place they possess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke defines solidity (or impenetrability) as that which hinders the approach of two bodies moved towards one another. He treats solidity as intimately connected with matter and explains its phenomenology (feeling support, resistance) and its role in distinguishing body from space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solidity fills space and is distinct from pure space
rubrics_metrics.description: Solidity is the idea whereby we conceive body to fill space, excluding other bodies; this idea is distinct from the idea of pure space, which has no resistance or protrusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explains that one can have an idea of motion or space without implying solidity; the idea of solidity involves resistance and exclusion of other bodies, unlike the abstract idea of space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solidity distinct from hardness
rubrics_metrics.description: Solidity (impenetrability) differs from hardness: solidity is repletion/exclusion of space, while hardness concerns cohesion of parts and resistance to change of figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke illustrates that soft bodies (e.g., water) can be as 'solid' in the sense of resisting intrusion as hard bodies, depending on how their parts behave under pressure; hardness is relative to our bodies' constitutions and sensations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solidity underlies impulse, resistance, and protrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: From the idea of solidity depend the notions of impulse, resistance, and protrusion; solidity is what distinguishes extension of body from extension of space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke links solidity to observable interactions among bodies and uses it to explain mechanical relations — how bodies keep others out of space they occupy and how that produces resistance and impulse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas received both by sight and touch: space, figure, rest, motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Some ideas (space or extension, figure, rest, and motion) make perceivable impressions both on the eyes and touch and can be received by either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These multisensory ideas will be treated more fully elsewhere, but Locke enumerates them as important simple ideas accessible by more than one sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple ideas of reflection: perception and willing
rubrics_metrics.description: When the mind turns inward and observes its own actions about ideas, it gets simple ideas from reflection such as PERCEPTION (thinking) and VOLITION (willing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke identifies the two principal internal operations that produce simple ideas by reflection and terms their capacities 'understanding' (thinking) and 'will' (volition). Later he will discuss modes like remembrance, reasoning, judging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas arising from both sensation and reflection (pleasure/pain, power, existence, unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain simple ideas (Pleasure/Delight and Pain/Uneasiness, Power, Existence, Unity) are suggested to the mind by both sensation and reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke notes these ideas pervade both external impressions and internal operations; they 'mix with almost all our other ideas' and are fundamental to motivation and ontology in his account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure and pain as motives of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure and pain are motives of our actions: nature attaches delight or uneasiness to thoughts and sensations to prompt choice, attention, and bodily action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explains the adaptive function: pleasure motivates pursuit, pain motivates avoidance; pain can warn of harm and thereby promote preservation, and the mixture of pleasure/pain leads humans to seek ultimate satisfaction beyond worldly goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of power and succession
rubrics_metrics.description: POWER is an idea derived from observing our own capacity to think and move and observing effects of bodies on one another; SUCCESSION is an idea suggested by the train of ideas in the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke treats these as simple ideas generated by both bodily experience and reflection on mental sequence — power as causal competence, succession as the serial order of ideas and events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive ideas can arise from privative causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever produces a perception in the mind yields a simple idea; even privations (absence of something) may produce positive ideas (e.g., darkness as privation of light).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke points out that ideas in the mind are considered as positive regardless of whether their external causes are positive qualities or privations; the understanding treats the idea itself without reference to the physical cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between ideas and their physical causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas in the mind are distinct from the qualities in things that give rise to them; one may have clear ideas (e.g., of colours) without understanding their physical causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke notes painters or dyers may have clearer ideas of colours than philosophers who theorize about causes; knowing an idea does not require knowledge of the external mechanism producing it.
